Background Research Utilized In Design Decisions
With the advancements in marine electric propulsion, different fields have found
applications for high speed craft. Two in particular are the militaristic and motorsport fields. The
main issues both of these fields are facing is reaching higher speeds while maintaining
maneuverability of the watercraft.

                     Background Research Utilized In Design Decisions

       With the advancements in marine electric propulsion, different fields have found

Many students on our team have an interest in motorsports. This interest heavily
influenced the design and ongoing modifications of the USV. This year's USV is a continuation
from last year’s USV. Our focus this year was to improve the efficiency of the USV and take it to
new speeds.
We wanted to design a hull that could be fast yet easy to maneuver at high speeds. We
designed different hulls in Fusion360 and then tested them using FEA and CFD. This led to us
making Pesce Volante, a catamaran style USV. In prior years, the team ran into issues of the
USV being overweight. This constrained how many people would be needed to test along with
needing more power to propel the USV. To solve this issue we wanted to use light weight
materials to construct the hull of the USV. After research, we decided to construct the frame of
the USV of foam to hold the shape while maintaining the buoyancy. We then wrapped the frame
with carbon fiber, to strengthen the hull.
For this year we wanted to improve the flow of water to the propellers. To do this we
wanted to improve the stern. We used CFD analysis to test different stern adjustments we could
possibly make. We shaped foam to match our desired shape from the CFD tests. This allowed
us to research and test many different sterns without damaging our hull or permanently
changing it before we had our desired outcome. Despite our best efforts, it was all for not. Our
breakthrough came from changing the propellers and not the stern.
As mentioned before, our team took inspiration from motorsports. One of these
inspirations is our active aero components that we install on our USV. At high speeds many
watercraft are unstable and this can become catastrophic. To combat this our team installed two
canards connected to servo motors to control the angle. The idea is that the canards will provide
extra lift or down force depending on the angle of attack of the USV. This idea came from
watching Formula 1’s Drag Reduction System (DRS). DRS allows the driver to control the
amount of drag depending on the needs of the race, more drag for turns and less drag for
straights. We tried to research if any watercraft have tried anything like a DRS system but failed
to find any.
One issue we ran into last year was the warping of our drivetrain. We are running
aluminum rods on the internal portion of our drivetrain. These rods were unconstrained other
than the stern wall and the motor. This led to the resonance when they were spinning at 4000
rpm, which caused them to permanently bend out of shape. We used FEA testing to start to
research ways to constrain the rod to prevent damaging the new ones.
Design Process
As mentioned previously this year's USV was a continuation from last year's team. This
year we were focused on maintaining,and improving our systems to ensure the highest
efficiency of our watercraft.
Energy Storage System
We are powering the USV with a single 48V for 60Ah battery. This is a huge update
from last year's craft which was powered by 4 Lithium Iron batteries that supplied 48V for
100Ah. By switching the power system, we were able to cut down almost 80lbs due to the
batteries. We chose a 60Ah battery when we learned the race was cut down from 5 miles to 2
miles for this year. We did not need a battery that had that much power.

Still the battery contains most of the weight of the USV;changing the location of the
battery causes major changes to how the USV sits and moves in the water. Last year we had a
high tech foam and ratchet system. We secured the battery in the boat with eight once inch
pieces of foam and a ratchet strap. While this allowed for easy moving of the battery’s location,
front and back, it was always a pain to lock into place. The easy movement of the battery
allowed us to test many different positions of the battery. It was important that we found the
most optimal position that helped the USV on a plane. Once we found the optimal position, we
set out to design and 3D print a cage for the battery. We constructed this cage for our design
and production.

Figure 1 - Battery Cage

We attached this to the USV with a high strength epoxy in our desired position allowing us to get
on a plane easier.

Active Aerodynamic Canards
To improve stability during acceleration and planing, we designed and implemented an active
aerodynamic control system using forward mounted canards. Unlike passive surfaces, this
system allows real time adjustment of canard angle based on the boat’s pitch, reducing
excessive bow rise during the transition to plane.

Active Aerodynamic Canards

To improve stability during acceleration and planing, we designed and implemented an active
aerodynamic control system using forward mounted canards. Unlike passive surfaces, this
system allows real time adjustment of canard angle based on the boat’s pitch, reducing
excessive bow rise during the transition to plane.

pages.text:
Figure 2 - Active Canard System Integration
Each canard is actuated by an independent 35 kg servo controlled through the Cube Orange
flight controller using a Lua script. The system reads pitch data from onboard sensors and
outputs corresponding PWM signals, allowing both canards to respond simultaneously. The use
of 7.5V servos required the implementation of a dedicated 7.5V power bus within the electrical
system to ensure consistent and reliable actuator performance.
A baseline linear relationship between pitch angle and canard position was established using
CFD and refined through testing. This provides sufficient downforce at low speeds while
minimizing drag at higher speeds. The goal of this implementation was to create a stable and
responsive baseline system that can be further developed. To validate the control logic, we
developed a small scale prototype integrating the telemetry system and canards. This enabled
rapid testing and tuning before full scale implementation.
The mechanical system was developed iteratively using additive manufacturing, primarily PETG
and PLA carbon fiber. A bearingless shaft design with greased tolerances was used to reduce
complexity and improve reliability in a marine environment, while multiple housing iterations
ensured proper servo placement and waterproofing.

Figure 3 - Canard Actuation Assembly
The final system provides a reliable and adaptable method of controlling hull attitude while
establishing a platform for future improvements in active aerodynamic control.
Drivetrain
When constructing our drive train, we wanted to choose a material that was light weight
yet durable and strong. This led us to choosing aluminum as our internal drive train shaft.
However, aluminum being a softer metal, started to deform and warp at 4000rpm. This led to the
damaging of our internal driveshaft material along with the potential risk of damaging the boat.
Using FEA tests we found that this was consistent with the resonant frequency of our shaft.

After further research and FEA test we found that the best way to prevent this was to constrain
the shaft. We designed and 3D printed a modular drive shaft stabilizer. The materials that were
used were Nylon-6 with carbon fiber reinforcements, PETG with carbon fiber, along with a
carbon fiber tube with radial ball bearings.

This stabilizer was attached to the USV using a high strength epoxy and has successfully
prevented warping and damage to the aluminum drive shaft.

Propeller Design: Pitch, Rake, and Blade Profile Optimization
       To improve thrust and overall propulsion efficiency, we designed and iterated on custom
propellers with a focus on pitch, rake, and blade profile. Early development primarily explored
increasing pitch to create more aggressive propellers; however, recent iterations have expanded

pages.text:
to include rake as a key design variable. The current design utilizes a rake angle of 20°, which
improves flow alignment and propeller loading under high speed conditions.
Figure 6 - Propeller Geometry with Increased Pitch and Rake
Blade geometry was also refined using hydrodynamic foil profiles with integrated cupping. This
design reduces tangential thrust losses and redirects flow more effectively in the axial direction,
improving overall thrust efficiency. The foil-based blade profile additionally reduces localized
stresses and improves performance under high RPM operation.

Figure 7 - Foil Blade Profile with Cupping
All propellers were developed through iterative additive manufacturing, allowing rapid testing of
multiple geometries. A range of materials were evaluated, including ABS, nylon, and carbon
fiber reinforced filaments. Through testing, PETG was identified as a highly effective material,
providing a balance of strength, print reliability, and surface quality. Despite initial expectations,
PETG propellers demonstrated sufficient durability under operating conditions of approximately
4000 RPM and speeds near 25 mph.
Current designs prioritize a combination of increased rake, optimized pitch, and hydrodynamic
blade shaping. While PETG remains the primary material, ongoing work includes investigating
composite reinforcement methods such as carbon fiber layups and embedded mesh structures
to further improve mechanical performance. This iterative approach has enabled the
development of propellers tailored to the USV’s operating conditions while establishing a
foundation for continued performance improvements.

Current Systems Design

Hull and Tracking
The hull is built around a catamaran-style planing body, a configuration selected after
modeling and simulation work indicated strong potential for high-speed planing performance
and maneuverability. This is the same hull from last years competition, as several hull concepts
in Fusion 360 and simulation-supported testing to settle on the catamaran layout proved the
best way to optimize simplicity and performance. The hull itself was conceived as a lightweight
but structurally capable platform, using carbon fiber as the primary structural material with foam
support to preserve form without unnecessary weight. A major area of hull focus this year has
been the stern region, where water is directed into the propellers. In testing, stern flow
refinement emerged as a central performance driver, as the quality of water entering the
propellers directly governs thrust consistency, cavitation behavior, and overall efficiency. Early
iterations incorporated shaped stern foam to provide rear buoyancy and guide flow into the
propellers, however, as propeller design was further refined, this approach proved unnecessary.
Instead, maintaining a pronounced stern cavity reduced drag while still allowing the hull to
achieve stable planing. By carefully shaping this cavity and controlling how water is delivered to
the propellers, the system sustains more consistent propeller loading at high speeds, mitigating
sputtering and improving effective thrust.

Figure 10 - Servo Controlled Rudder Configuration
slower-spinning propeller to generate turning authority through asymmetric thrust, which
increases hydrodynamic drag and reduces propulsive symmetry. In contrast, the current rudder
arrangement allows both propellers to run at equal RPM while the rudder provides directional
control across a 90° range (±45° from center), significantly tightening the turning radius. The
rudder assembly was also designed to be modular and adjustable, allowing the team to tune
immersion depth and steering response while preserving alignment at speed.
An active aerodynamic canard has been integrated at the bow to enhance both planing
performance and high-speed stability. The canard is servo-controlled, allowing it to dynamically
adjust its angle based on operating conditions. During acceleration, it generates additional
downforce at the front of the vessel, helping the hull transition onto plane more efficiently by
counteracting bow rise. At higher speeds, the system continues to regulate pitch by providing
controlled aerodynamic loading, reducing the likelihood of excessive attack angles and
improving overall stability. Unlike a fixed surface, the active canard allows the vessel to adapt in
real time, making it a key component in maintaining consistent performance across different
speed regimes.

pages.text:
continuing through the distribution system to the ESCs, pumps, and supporting electronics. A
7.5V and a 12V voltage converter was also used to step down power for the onboard telemetry
system. This year, the same general architecture is maintained, but with a simplified
configuration. Instead of using four Lithium Iron batteries to supply 48V at 100Ah, the system
now relies on a single battery ‘box’. This reduces overall system complexity, improves
packaging/weight distribution, and streamlines power delivery without changing the core design.

Figure 13 - Main Power Storage: Battery ‘Box’
As mentioned before, this year, during testing, we also observed noticeable electrical
interference between the motor wires, ESCs, and microcontrollers. Much of this was due to
long, bundled wiring runs, which introduced noise and caused inconsistencies between
controller input and actual power output. To address this, the electronics were reorganized using
custom 3D-printed mounting boards, and wire lengths were shortened and better separated.
These changes improved signal clarity and resulted in more stable and predictable system
performance.
Supporting electronics are also intentionally kept concise in the overall design narrative,
but they still play an important role. The Orange Cube flight controller is at the center of the
vessel’s sensing and control architecture, interfacing with GPS, IMUs, magnetometers, and
other peripherals while running ArduPilot for telemetry and control logic. In practice, this gives
our team a compact way to monitor USV attitude, path tracking, speed, and system response
during testing.

Figure 14 - Simplified Circuitry
Motor and Drive Train
The propulsion system is built around two electric motors drawing from a shared power
system, transmitting torque through a dual-shaft drivetrain. Each side uses a three-shaft
configuration connected by U-joints, allowing the drivetrain to follow a stepped geometry: angled
downward from the motor, transitioning to horizontal, and then pitched slightly downward again
(≈3°) with an inward toe of about 5°. This arrangement optimizes thrust alignment while
accommodating the spatial constraints of the hull. The shafts, originally developed last year and
improved upon this year were retained and refined for their light weight, ease of machining, and
low rotational inertia, with the U-joints enabling smooth power transfer across the changing
angles between the motors and stern assembly. During testing this year, however, significant
shaft whipping was observed in the central sections at higher speeds. To address this, a 5-inch
ball-bearing shaft stabilizer was introduced, which is mounted to the bottom of the USV. This
addition reduced shaft deflection by more than half and produced noticeably smoother, more
stable rotation under load, particularly at high RPM.
Propeller geometry was one of the most heavily iterated aspects of the design. The final
configuration features a cupped blade profile with increased rake and pitch, which redirects the
thrust vector more linearly rather than radially outward, a limitation observed in earlier designs.
Thrust efficiency is governed by blade count, pitch, and diameter, and iterative testing allowed
the propulsion system to converge on an optimized surface-piercing configuration. A key
takeaway is that the drivetrain and propeller system were developed as an integrated unit rather

angles between the motors and stern assembly. During testing this year, however, significant

addition reduced shaft deflection by more than half and produced noticeably smoother, more

        Propeller geometry was one of the most heavily iterated aspects of the design. The final
configuration features a cupped blade profile with increased rake and pitch, which redirects the
thrust vector more linearly rather than radially outward, a limitation observed in earlier designs.
Thrust efficiency is governed by blade count, pitch, and diameter, and iterative testing allowed
the propulsion system to converge on an optimized surface-piercing configuration. A key
takeaway is that the drivetrain and propeller system were developed as an integrated unit rather

pages.text:
than as separate components. Shaft angle, stern flow, motor output, and propeller loading are
all tightly coupled, and performance depends on how well these elements work together.

Figure 15 - Pesce Volate 15 kW Motor

Cooling System
The cooling system remains one of the most important elements of our design. The USV
uses a closed-loop water-cooling approach built around two pumps and two onboard reservoirs,
with ice water routed through the motors and electronic speed controllers before recirculating.
Additionally we went through tubing improvements in mounting the tubes to the inner walls of
the hull to prevent kinking and preserve uninterrupted flow, which is critical in a closed-loop
system where any restriction directly reduces cooling effectiveness. This architecture avoids
dependence on raw external water pickup and gives the team a controlled thermal environment
during a race run.

Figure 16 - Pesce Volante Cooling Pump

                                Figure 15 - Pesce Volate 15 kW Motor


Cooling System

        The cooling system remains one of the most important elements of our design. The USV
uses a closed-loop water-cooling approach built around two pumps and two onboard reservoirs,
with ice water routed through the motors and electronic speed controllers before recirculating.
Additionally we went through tubing improvements in mounting the tubes to the inner walls of
the hull to prevent kinking and preserve uninterrupted flow, which is critical in a closed-loop
system where any restriction directly reduces cooling effectiveness. This architecture avoids
dependence on raw external water pickup and gives the team a controlled thermal environment
during a race run.

Risks and Mitigations
During the fabrication and integration of the USV, potential risks were identified across
all major subsystems. The team has implemented mitigation strategies where possible and
outlined areas requiring continued testing and validation. The primary risks and corresponding
mitigation approaches are as follows:

Power Storage
The electrical system presents risks related to excessive current draw and thermal
overload. To mitigate this, the battery system is protected by both a fuse and a thermal circuit
breaker. These safeguards are designed to automatically interrupt power in the event of
abnormal current or overheating, preventing damage to critical components and reducing the
risk of system failure.

External Control System
Wiring connections between internal and external electronics are vulnerable to
mechanical stress, potential disconnection, and EMF interference. To address this, the external
electronics housing incorporates a clamped wire interface that secures all connections, as well
as aluminum shielded wiring to reduce interference. This design reduces strain on the wiring
and minimizes the likelihood of detachment, ensuring consistent control of the vessel during
operation.

Propulsion System
The propulsion system introduces risks associated with mechanical loading, vibration,
and component fatigue. Testing has shown that the propellers generate significant axial and
radial loads on the motors (as shown by previous prop models shearing near the axes of
rotation). To mitigate this, thrust bearings are being implemented within the external drivetrain
supports to better manage these loads, as well as reinforced propeller center points.
Additionally, motor mounts are reinforced by integrating them into carbon fiber structural
elements within the hull. This reduces vibration-induced movement and lowers the risk of motor
detachment under high-speed operation.

components such as wiring. To mitigate this, a custom damping system was designed and

RPMs without exponential risk.

Cooling System
There is a risk that the cooling system may be insufficient to remove heat generated by
the motors and electronic speed controllers, potentially leading to overheating. This risk is being
addressed through continued system testing to evaluate thermal performance under varying
operating conditions, including scenarios with and without ice-assisted cooling. The ice water
cooling loop and air ventilation system are designed to function together, providing redundancy
in heat dissipation. While simultaneous failure of both systems is unlikely, further testing is being
conducted to validate reliability and determine optimal operating parameters.

Water Ingress
The addition of bow and stern vents/hatches introduces the possibility of water entering
the hull and compromising onboard electronics. Because this is a relatively new design feature,
the extent of this risk is still being evaluated through iterative testing. If water ingress is
observed, it will be mitigated through additional sealing, including the application of waterproof
sealants at critical interfaces. Ongoing testing will determine whether further structural
adjustments are required.

Hull Damage
The hull is constructed from carbon fiber and resin, providing strong resistance to shear
forces but limited resistance to puncture. Impacts with debris or obstacles could compromise
hull integrity and allow water ingress. This risk is mitigated through careful piloting and real-time
visibility provided by onboard camera systems used during testing. Additionally, material testing
has shown that the reinforced carbon fiber layup offers sufficient durability for expected race
conditions, reducing the likelihood of damage from normal operational loads.

Propeller Damage
The propellers are subject to potential damage from both external impacts and excessive
torque at high speeds. This risk is being addressed through iterative testing to determine the
mechanical limits of the propellers and drivetrain system. Torque testing and on-water trials are
used to establish safe operating thresholds. The vessel will not be operated beyond these limits,
ensuring that both propeller integrity and drivetrain reliability are maintained.

Loss of Remote Signal (Failsafe Control)

        A loss of remote signal presents the risk of the vessel continuing uncontrolled operation.
This issue has been mitigated through the implementation of an automatic stop failsafe within

pages.text:
the control script. In the event of signal loss, the system immediately cuts power to the motors,
ensuring the vessel does not continue moving without operator control.

GPS Data Integrity
The navigation and telemetry system relies on GPS data, which introduces the risk of
corrupted or missing signals. This could impact path tracking and system awareness. To
mitigate this, the control system is designed to handle inconsistent data inputs and rely on
additional onboard sensors, such as IMUs and magnetometers, to maintain stability and provide
fallback state estimation when GPS data is unreliable.

Excessive Attack Angle (Flip Risk)
At high speeds and during the planing phase, the vessel is susceptible to excessive
pitch angles, which can increase the risk of instability or flipping. This risk is mitigated through a
combination of hull design, weight distribution, and control system monitoring. The catamaran
geometry provides inherent stability, while sensor feedback allows the system to detect and
respond to unsafe pitch conditions during operation. Continued testing (PID included) is used to
refine operating limits and ensure stable planing behavior across speed regimes.
